raw_lines: In a single morning, 20,000 people died
where they stood.
No war killed them. No plague emptied
their streets. The mountain did it.
This is Pompeii, the city that time
forgot to destroy. And today, we are
walking its streets again.
I am standing in the forum, where
senators once argued and merchants
shouted their prices.
The paving stones still carry the ruts
of cart wheels, worn deep over
centuries.
What amazes me is this.
I am walking the exact road a Roman
walked on the exact morning he died.
But before the mountain speaks, let me
ask you something.
If you had 4 hours to live, what would
you grab?
Your money? Your family? Your memories?
Keep that question in your pocket.
Because at 1:00 in the afternoon on an
ordinary summer day, Pompeii ran out of
time.
Rewind 2,000 years. The Bay of Naples
glitters below. Pompeii is rich, loud,
and alive. 20,000 people pack its
streets. Sailors, wine merchants,
bakers, gladiators, ships crowd the
harbor with oil and grain. This is not
some forgotten village. This is a Roman
boomtown. Morning in Pompeii smells like
fresh bread. 150 thermopolia, the fast
food counters of Rome, serve hot stew to
workers in a hurry.
In the bakery, 80 loaves slide into the
brick ovens. And the amphitheater, the
oldest surviving one in the Roman world,
roars with 20,000 voices. Wealth paints
